Chapter 4: Prioritizing What Matters—Managing Time and Energy Effectively.
Now that you've got a clear vision in mind, the real challenge is making sure your daily actions actually line up with those long-term priorities.
Let’s talk about what it really means to put first things first—organizing your time and energy around what’s most important, not just what feels urgent in the moment.
In a world where being busy often gets mistaken for being productive, this can feel like a pretty radical shift, right?
Here’s the big insight: not all tasks are created equal. Some things you do each day push you closer to your meaningful goals or reflect your core values. Others? Well, they're just distractions, or maybe they’re things you do because someone else is asking—not because they truly matter to you.
Highly effective people learn to spot the difference between what’s truly important and what simply feels urgent.
One tool that really helps with this is the time management matrix. Imagine breaking your activities into four categories:
First, there’s Important and Urgent—think crises, pressing problems, or last-minute projects.
Then, Important but Not Urgent—this is planning, relationship-building, personal growth, and prevention.
Next, Not Important but Urgent—interruptions, some emails or calls, those minor requests that pop up.
And finally, Not Important and Not Urgent—the true time-wasters, those trivial activities that eat up your day.
Here’s something to pay attention to: the smartest way to use your time is to focus on activities that are important but not urgent. These are the things that build your skills, strengthen your relationships, and help prevent future problems.
But because they don’t shout for your attention, they’re often the first to get left behind.
So, how do you actually prioritize what matters? Here are a few practical strategies:
Start with weekly planning. Set aside time each week to review your goals and schedule the key things that really matter.
Use delegation—hand off tasks to others when it makes sense, so you can free up your time for higher priorities.
And don’t be afraid to say no. It’s okay to politely turn down requests that don’t fit with your values or your main goals.
Picture a parent who truly values quality time with their family, but finds the whole week swallowed up by work and errands. By intentionally setting aside time just for family—and guarding it that way—the parent makes sure what matters most doesn’t get pushed aside by less important demands.
Remember, this habit isn’t about creating a rigid schedule or cramming more tasks into your day. It’s about making conscious choices—investing your time and energy where it’ll have the most positive impact.
Sometimes, it takes courage to say no to good opportunities, so you can say yes to the best ones.
Over time, you’ll notice life starts to feel more balanced and fulfilling. Instead of just reacting to whatever’s urgent, you’re acting with intention—guided by what’s truly important to you.
That’s really the heart of effective self-management.
